newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil re-election foes gather to discuss strategy.
newsitem.headline: Brazil re-election foes gather to discuss strategy.

text.p: Left and right-wing opponents of Brazilian President Fernando Henrique Cardoso's re-election plan held a last-minute meeting to discuss how to block today's first vote on a re-election bill in the Chamber of Deputies.
Despite their different ideologies, the party leaders were united in disputing the government's claims that it had more than the 308 votes needed to approve the amendment.
"What is clear is that we have more than enough support to block and stop the voting," Dep. Jose Machado, lower house leader of the socialist Workers Party told national Globo television.

"The government is hugely overestimating its numbers," said Dep. Antonio Delfim Netto, an ex-finance minister and a friend of Paulo Maluf, a former Sao Paulo mayor who hopes to defeat Cardoso's re-election plan and boost his own presidential plans.

Maluf, recovering at home in Sao Paulo from an operation to remove his prostrate gland, accused Cardoso of attempting to change the constitution purely for his own benefit and told Globo only 265 deputies would vote in favor of the re-election bill.

The opponents of Cardoso's re-election, including a rebel faction of the Brazilian Democratic Movement Party (PMDB), the largest in Congress, which is split over the re-election bid, hopes to stall tonight's scheduled vote by not registering their presence in the lower house.

Voting on constitutional amendments may only begin once 308 deputies register and the opposition's tactic would force the government to make sure its supporters turn out en masse to begin proceedings and then remain for voting.

The opposition also plans to put forward proposed changes to the re-election amendment which, if approved, would oblige the government to call a plebiscite on the issue and make Cardoso step down from office if involved in a re-election campaign.
While the opposition discussed its tactics, leaders of government-allied parties insisted they had enough votes.
"We're gathering more and more votes as time goes by...We're certain of victory," Benito Gama, the government's leader in the lower house said.
